item.title: 22 Oct 2026
item.description:
Porphurios makes the point in his letter to his wife Marcella that, while it is difficult to force people to wear fetters of iron, if you give them the (much heavier!) fetters of gold, they will wear them willingly.

What would he think, I wonder, of the plastic and silicon fetters that people wear today?

item.title: 16 Oct 2026: Bouncy Castle
item.description:
οὐδὲν ἀκιδνότερον γαῖα τρέφει
Earth breeds nothing more pathetic than ἀνθρώποιο,
a human,

πάντων ὅσσα τε
of all the things that γαῖαν ἔπι
on Earth πνείει
breathe τε καὶ
and ἕρπει.
creep:*

οὐ μὲν γάρ ποτέ φησι
for he never expects κακὸν πείσεσθαι
to suffer misfortune ὀπίσσω,
later on

ὄφρ’
so long as ἀρετὴν παρέχωσι θεοὶ
the gods grant prosperity καὶ
and γούνατ’
his knees ὀρώρῃ:
move;*

ἀλλ’
but ὅτε δὴ
as soon as καὶ λυγρὰ θεοὶ μάκαρες τελέσωσι,
the blessed gods also bring about miseries,

καὶ τὰ φέρει
he bears these too, ἀεκαζόμενος
unwillingly, τετληότι
suffering θυμῷ:
at heart.

τοῖος γὰρ
For such νόος ἐστὶν
is the mind ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων
of earthbound humans:

οἷον
however ἐπ’ ἦμαρ
on a given day ἄγησι πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε.
the father of men and gods leads it.

  1. creep: cf. Ilias XVII 446–7.
  2. his knees move: that is, while he has strength.

(Homeros, Odusseia XVIII 130–7.)

This has been a tricky week for me, awakening with spirits bright one day and crushed the next. I was talking with a friend earlier who has been experiencing similarly, so perhaps it is something in the air... if you are also on the roller coaster, may you find evenness and peace.

item.title: 12 Oct 2026: Why Ganumedes Was Spirited Away
item.description:
An eternity ago, when I was wrapping up my Plotinos series, I wrote:

I recognize Plotinos isn’t for everyone. Indeed, Neoplatonism is so obviously not a religion for most people that it’s no wonder at all to me that it died out and was replaced with one that was! No, this is a very peculiar way of understanding the cosmos, only really suited to peculiar people.

It came up a couple times recently, and so I wanted to hazard an attempt at unpacking why this ought to be the case.

Let’s take the seven degrees of consciousness as a series of classrooms, each having a lesson to learn: elements learn to be, animals learn to grow, humans learn to identify, heroes learn to love, daimones learn to understand, angels learn to universalize, gods learn to unify. (I am using Hierokles of Alexandria’s terminology for the beings of each degree of consciousness, rather than my usual four-fold terminology, here.)

Let’s suppose we have a student in the human classroom, attempting to learn how to have an identity—that is, attempting to learn how to relate to the group. But humans have free will: let us suppose that the others in the classroom are peculiarly hostile to our poor student, defining them as an outsider, and shutting them out of social interaction. This is beneficial for the hostile students, of course, since such identification allows them to better develop their own identities, but it is harmful to the one student, since it prevents them from doing so. So what are they to do?

Well, perhaps the obvious option is to try to find some other group to engage with, or else develop some identity so compelling or disruptive that the others find it impossible to ignore: this would restore balance, and all the students would then continue to develop as normal.

But let us suppose that the shutting out of our student is sufficiently complete, and that the student is sufficiently discouraged and precocious, that, rather than continuing to attempt to engage with the group, they instead go on to develop their higher capacities: perhaps they try to learn compassion for the group that has so shunned them, or perhaps they try to understand the mechanics behind why things are the way they are, or so on. This is commendable, but now we have a problem! See, the student has failed to learn the lessons of their grade, and so they lack the prerequisites necessary to graduate to the next: even if they advanced, they would be unable to effectively learn the lessons there. But on the other hand, one can’t simply hold them back and make them repeat their grade: they have already moved beyond it, their interests lie elsewhere, to hold them back would be to punish them for the actions of others, for working hard, for trying to learn; this would simply discourage them from trying to learn in the future, which is the whole point of their existence! So the student has made a paradox for themselves: they can’t move on, but neither can they stay where they are.

What to do?

In an ideal world, perhaps the compassionate thing would be to pull the student out of school and give them a tutor who can specialize the curriculum to their peculiar needs, yes? And this is why, I think, Ganumedes, with his peculiar beauty, is judged unfit to live with either of his brothers and so is snatched up to Olumpos in a whirlwind; or why heroes, betrayed by Mother Earth, murder her so that they may be judged illegitimate to her and instead inherit Father Sky’s kingdom.

So, then, speculative philosophies like the mystery schools or Neoplatonism aren’t meant for everyone. Perhaps it is correct to say, as most kinds of spirituality do, that it is best to learn to appreciate earth and live well in it; but one must recognize that this is sometimes impossible, and so it is also best, in such cases, for one “to try to escape from earth to the dwelling of the gods as quickly as one can.”

item.title: 26 Sep 2026
item.description: Reflecting back on this post from a couple years ago, a fourth, and frankly more obvious, possibility has occurred to me: Apollon is simply suggesting that, as Puthagoras was the dawn of Greek philosophy, and Plato its zenith, so too was Plotinos its twilight.

item.title: 31 Aug 2026
item.description:
Stumbled across a quote worth remembering in an otherwise uninteresting article:

When a human being becomes exhausted after making all possible sincere efforts, and cries out in despair, the highest state of devotion emerges. And during that spontaneous devotional flood, the student attains ecstasy. That is called the grace of God. In a sense this grace is unconditional, but it is still the fruit of faithful and sincere effort.
